title: Biological Techniques
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Biological Techniques curriculum: microscopy, specimen preparation and sectioning, staining, fixation/preservation, basic laboratory chemistry (chromatography, spectrophotometry), herbarium and field sampling methods, and sterile/aseptic technique.

questions.question: The total magnification of a compound light microscope is calculated by:
options: Multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece (ocular) lens by the magnification of the objective lens in use
Adding the eyepiece and objective magnifications together
Dividing the objective magnification by the eyepiece magnification
Using the objective lens magnification alone
questions.correct_answer: Multiplying the magnification of the eyepiece (ocular) lens by the magnification of the objective lens in use
questions.explanation: Total magnification equals eyepiece magnification times objective magnification, e.g. a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective gives 400x total magnification.

questions.question: The resolving power of a light microscope refers to its ability to:
options: Distinguish two closely spaced points as separate rather than as one blurred point
Magnify an object to any desired size
Change the colour of the specimen
questions.correct_answer: Distinguish two closely spaced points as separate rather than as one blurred point
questions.explanation: Resolution (resolving power) is the capacity to show two nearby structures as distinct, which is limited by the wavelength of light used and is distinct from magnification.

questions.question: For examining very small or fine internal structures within a light microscope's resolution limits, a specimen is usually first prepared by:
options: Sectioning it into thin slices using a microtome
Freezing it in liquid nitrogen without slicing
Viewing it whole without any preparation
questions.correct_answer: Sectioning it into thin slices using a microtome
questions.explanation: A microtome cuts tissue into very thin sections thin enough for light to pass through, which is necessary for detailed microscopic examination of internal structure.

questions.question: Before a plant tissue sample can be sectioned on a microtome, it is typically first fixed and then embedded in a supporting medium such as:
questions.correct_answer: Paraffin wax
questions.explanation: In the paraffin embedding method, dehydrated tissue is infiltrated with and embedded in paraffin wax, which provides the firm support needed for cutting very thin, uniform sections.

questions.question: The main purpose of fixation (e.g., using formalin-acetic-alcohol, FAA) in tissue preparation is to:
options: Preserve cellular structure and stop autolysis/decay as close to the living state as possible
Add colour to the specimen for viewing
Increase the size of the cells
questions.correct_answer: Preserve cellular structure and stop autolysis/decay as close to the living state as possible
questions.explanation: Fixation rapidly kills and hardens tissue while preserving cell and tissue architecture, preventing enzymatic degradation (autolysis) and microbial decay before further processing.

questions.question: Before embedding in paraffin wax, fixed plant tissue must pass through a graded series of increasing alcohol concentrations. This step is called:
questions.correct_answer: Dehydration
questions.explanation: Dehydration gradually removes water from the tissue using an ascending alcohol series, which is essential because wax (and most clearing agents) are not miscible with water.

questions.question: Safranin is a stain commonly used in plant microtechnique to selectively colour:
options: Lignified and cutinised cell walls (and nuclei) a red colour
questions.correct_answer: Lignified and cutinised cell walls (and nuclei) a red colour
questions.explanation: Safranin is commonly paired with fast green in double-staining protocols; safranin stains lignified/cutinised tissues and nuclei red, while fast green stains cellulose walls and cytoplasm.

questions.question: In the safranin-fast green double staining technique for plant sections, fast green primarily stains:
options: Cellulose cell walls and cytoplasm, appearing green
questions.correct_answer: Cellulose cell walls and cytoplasm, appearing green
questions.explanation: Fast green counterstains non-lignified, cellulose-rich walls and cytoplasm green, providing contrast against the red-stained lignified elements from safranin.

questions.question: Iodine (iodine-potassium iodide, I2KI) solution is commonly used in the laboratory as a simple stain to detect the presence of:
questions.correct_answer: Starch, which turns blue-black
questions.explanation: Iodine solution forms a characteristic blue-black complex with amylose in starch, making it a simple and widely used test for starch presence.

questions.question: A temporary wet mount slide for light microscopy is typically prepared by placing the specimen on a slide, adding a drop of mounting fluid, and then:
options: Lowering a coverslip at an angle to avoid trapping air bubbles
Dropping the coverslip flat and fast from a height
Sealing the slide immediately with nail varnish before viewing
Heating the slide directly over an open flame
questions.correct_answer: Lowering a coverslip at an angle to avoid trapping air bubbles
questions.explanation: Lowering the coverslip slowly at an angle allows the mounting fluid to spread evenly and pushes air out ahead of it, minimising trapped air bubbles that would obscure the view.

questions.question: The technique of separating plant tissue into its individual component cells (e.g., to study xylem vessel elements or fibres) by softening the middle lamella, typically using a mixture such as chromic and nitric acid, is called:
questions.correct_answer: Maceration
questions.explanation: Maceration dissolves the pectin-rich middle lamella holding cells together, allowing individual cell types (like tracheids or fibres) to be separated and studied.

questions.question: The instrument fitted inside a compound microscope's eyepiece and used to measure the actual size of microscopic objects is the:
questions.correct_answer: Ocular micrometer
questions.explanation: An ocular micrometer is a small scale placed in the eyepiece; it must be calibrated against a stage micrometer (a known scale on a slide) before it can give real measurements.

questions.question: Calibrating an ocular micrometer against a stage micrometer is necessary because:
options: The value of each ocular division changes depending on which objective lens magnification is being used
The ocular micrometer never needs recalibration once set
Stage micrometers cannot be used with compound microscopes
Calibration only matters for electron microscopes
questions.correct_answer: The value of each ocular division changes depending on which objective lens magnification is being used
questions.explanation: Because total magnification changes with each objective lens, the real distance represented by one ocular micrometer division must be recalibrated for every objective used.

questions.question: A dissecting (stereo) microscope, compared to a compound microscope, is generally preferred for:
options: Examining whole, relatively large, opaque specimens at low magnification with a three-dimensional view
Viewing extremely thin, transparent sections at very high magnification
questions.correct_answer: Examining whole, relatively large, opaque specimens at low magnification with a three-dimensional view
questions.explanation: Dissecting microscopes provide lower magnification but a wider field of view, greater working distance, and stereoscopic (3D) imaging, ideal for manipulating and examining whole specimens.

questions.question: In paper chromatography, the Rf (retention factor) value of a compound is calculated as:
options: Distance travelled by the compound divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front
Distance travelled by the solvent front divided by the distance travelled by the compound
Total time of the run in minutes
The concentration of the compound in the original sample
questions.correct_answer: Distance travelled by the compound divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front, a characteristic, reproducible value (under fixed conditions) used to help identify a compound.

questions.question: A pigment spot travels 6 cm while the solvent front travels 10 cm on a chromatography paper. The Rf value of the pigment is:
questions.explanation: Rf = distance travelled by pigment / distance travelled by solvent = 6 cm / 10 cm = 0.6.

questions.question: Paper chromatography is commonly used in plant biology laboratory practicals to:
options: Separate and identify plant pigments such as chlorophylls and carotenoids
questions.correct_answer: Separate and identify plant pigments such as chlorophylls and carotenoids
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates a pigment mixture (e.g., a leaf extract) into its components based on differential solubility and adsorption, allowing individual pigments to be identified.

questions.question: Beer-Lambert's law, applied in spectrophotometry, states that the absorbance of a solution is:
options: Directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing substance and the path length of light through it
Unrelated to the concentration of the solute
Only dependent on the colour of the container
questions.correct_answer: Directly proportional to the concentration of the absorbing substance and the path length of light through it
questions.explanation: Beer-Lambert's law (A = εcl) states absorbance is directly proportional to molar absorptivity, concentration, and path length, allowing unknown concentrations to be determined from absorbance readings.

questions.question: A spectrophotometer is used in biological laboratories mainly to:
options: Measure the amount of light absorbed or transmitted by a solution at a specific wavelength
questions.correct_answer: Measure the amount of light absorbed or transmitted by a solution at a specific wavelength
questions.explanation: Spectrophotometers quantify light absorbance/transmittance through a sample at chosen wavelengths, widely used to estimate concentrations of pigments, proteins, and other biomolecules.

questions.question: Sterilisation of culture media and laboratory equipment by moist heat under pressure is achieved using a(n):
questions.correct_answer: Autoclave
questions.explanation: An autoclave uses pressurised steam, typically at 121 degrees Celsius and 15 psi for about 15-20 minutes, to kill microorganisms and spores effectively, sterilising media and equipment.

questions.question: Aseptic technique in microbiological or tissue culture work is used primarily to:
options: Prevent contamination of cultures and samples by unwanted microorganisms
Increase the colour intensity of stains
questions.correct_answer: Prevent contamination of cultures and samples by unwanted microorganisms
questions.explanation: Aseptic technique (sterile handling, flaming instruments, working near a flame or in a laminar flow hood) minimises the introduction of contaminating bacteria, fungi, or other microbes into pure cultures.

questions.question: In a laboratory titration to determine the concentration of an unknown acid solution using a standard base, the point at which the reaction is exactly complete is called the:
questions.correct_answer: Equivalence (end) point
questions.explanation: The equivalence point in a titration is reached when the amount of titrant added exactly reacts with the substance being analysed, often indicated by a colour change from an indicator.

questions.question: A pH meter is used in the laboratory to:
options: Measure the hydrogen ion concentration (acidity or alkalinity) of a solution
Measure the temperature of a solution
Determine the molecular weight of a compound
questions.correct_answer: Measure the hydrogen ion concentration (acidity or alkalinity) of a solution
questions.explanation: A pH meter uses a glass electrode sensitive to hydrogen ion activity to give a precise, quantitative reading of a solution's pH.

questions.question: A buffer solution used in the laboratory functions to:
options: Resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
questions.correct_answer: Resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
questions.explanation: Buffers consist of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or vice versa) and maintain a relatively stable pH, which is essential for many biological experiments and enzyme assays.

questions.question: Centrifugation is a laboratory technique used to:
options: Separate components of a mixture based on differences in density using centrifugal force
Measure the pH of a solution
questions.correct_answer: Separate components of a mixture based on differences in density using centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Centrifugation spins samples at high speed, causing denser components to sediment faster than less dense ones, allowing separation of cell organelles, precipitates, or immiscible layers.

questions.question: When weighing chemicals precisely for making a stock solution, the most appropriate instrument to use is a(n):
questions.correct_answer: Analytical (electronic) balance
questions.explanation: An analytical balance provides highly precise mass measurements (often to 0.0001 g), essential for accurately preparing reagents and solutions of known concentration.

questions.question: In a classic osmosis demonstration using potato strips placed in distilled water versus concentrated salt solution, the strips placed in distilled water become:
options: Firmer and increase slightly in mass/length as water enters by osmosis
Flaccid and decrease in mass/length as water leaves
Unchanged, since potato tissue is impermeable to water
questions.correct_answer: Firmer and increase slightly in mass/length as water enters by osmosis
questions.explanation: Since distilled water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the potato cell sap, water moves into the cells by osmosis, making the tissue firmer and slightly heavier/longer.

questions.question: In field vegetation sampling, a square or rectangular sampling frame of fixed area used to estimate plant species density, frequency, or cover is called a:
questions.correct_answer: Quadrat
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a standard-sized frame placed at sample points to systematically record the plants present, allowing quantitative comparison across a study area.

questions.question: The line transect method in ecological field sampling involves:
options: Stretching a measuring tape/line across the study area and recording species touching or crossing it at set intervals
Randomly scattering quadrats with no fixed pattern
Using only satellite imagery for data collection
Weighing all plant material in a plot
questions.correct_answer: Stretching a measuring tape/line across the study area and recording species touching or crossing it at set intervals
questions.explanation: A line transect records species that intersect a fixed line across a habitat, often used to study zonation or gradients such as changes from a water body outward.

questions.question: When preparing a herbarium specimen, the plant press is typically composed of alternating layers of specimen, blotting/newspaper, and:
options: Corrugated cardboard sheets (ventilators) to allow airflow during drying
Wet cotton wool to keep the specimen moist
Aluminium foil to block all light
questions.correct_answer: Corrugated cardboard sheets (ventilators) to allow airflow during drying
questions.explanation: Corrugated cardboard ventilators between layers of blotting paper allow air to circulate through the stack, speeding even drying and reducing fungal spoilage of the specimen.

questions.question: Culture media used to grow microorganisms in the laboratory (e.g., nutrient agar) must be sterilised before inoculation mainly to:
options: Eliminate pre-existing microorganisms that would otherwise contaminate and outcompete the intended culture
Increase the nutrient content of the medium
Change the colour of the medium for easier viewing
questions.correct_answer: Eliminate pre-existing microorganisms that would otherwise contaminate and outcompete the intended culture
questions.explanation: Sterilising the medium (typically by autoclaving) kills any existing microbes so that only the deliberately introduced (inoculated) organism grows in pure culture.

questions.question: Basic laboratory safety practice dictates that when diluting concentrated acid with water, one should always:
options: Add acid slowly to water, never water to concentrated acid
Add water rapidly to concentrated acid
Mix acid and water in equal volumes without regard to order
Heat the acid strongly before mixing
questions.correct_answer: Add acid slowly to water, never water to concentrated acid
questions.explanation: Adding acid to water allows the heat of dilution to dissipate safely into the larger volume of water; adding water to concentrated acid can cause violent, dangerous spattering.

questions.question: The correct sequence of general steps in preparing a stained, temporary plant tissue slide for microscopy is:
questions.correct_answer: Sectioning, staining, mounting, and observation
questions.explanation: A thin section is first cut, then stained to highlight structures, then mounted on a slide under a coverslip in a suitable medium, and finally examined under the microscope.
